Avocados: The Superfood Thieves.

By: ALTYDVRYSTAAT PRODUCTIONS | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The avocado farming industry buckles under massive pressure due to large scale avocado stealing syndicate.

Unique Selling Point:
Inside information from security company

Summary:
The avocado farming industry are under massive pressure due to large scale theft of their produce. Since 2009, total plantings of Avocado in SA has increased due to a growing customer demand. SA produces more than 120,000 tonnes of avos annually - about 58% of our Avocados are grown in Limpopo Province

To prepare land for the planting of avo’s the cost (including the planting itself and spraying of the trees) can run as much as R350 000 per hectare.
Further production costs from seedling to harvest will run as much as R51 000 per hectare.
A ton of stolen avo’s (depending on market prices at the time) can mean about R50 000 disappearing from a farmer’s cash flow.
One ton can disappear in a single evening. But how possible is it to steal that large an amount of fruit?
We will interview some farmers, as well as someone from the Avo-growers Association to discuss the modus operandi of the thieves and the implications on the industry.


Introduction to viewers: * Link with Claire — making smashed avo on toast — explaining that Avocado is a superfood, popular with health conscious, weight watchers and plant-based eaters… And also… poachers…

Further information:
With limited police resources,Canine Security is a wonderful outfit in the Tzaneen area. They have established a WhatsApp group for residents and respond to every call for help sent out on the group, regardless of whether the complainant is a customer of theirs or not.
They have the same attitude to the farming community. We will talk to their two owners about their nightly battles against fruit thieves.
A major problem in this is the fruit stalls next to our roads. A large percentage of these fruit sellers are alleged to buy from the thieves. At the moment, in that area no avo’s are ready to be picked.

We will have a farmer show us how to recognize avo’s that were picked too early. - Nelius Human


We will also speak to some of the informal traders, finding out where they get their avos and how much they make from the sale of their avos.





Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Tzaneen
415 Km's x 2
150 Km's travel between the farms in Tzaneen
Total 565km's x R3.50 = R1977.50

Total R850 pp per night
R3400.00

Press Release:


Greengold on the Black Market

Rich in nutrients and oils, avocados became the superfood of dieters, sport stars and trendy eateries in the last decade. Being high demand has meant the price has skyrocketed and that has spelled quick money for criminals cashing in on an increasingly easy access to what some nor call “green gold”. With ready markets in towns and cities, it’s in avo heartland where large-scale loot originates. Carte Blanche travels to Tzaneen in the Limpopo Province where virtually every farmer has been affected and we meet the small, but savvy army of private security and their blood hounds that are taking the fight to the green gold poachers.

Producer: Niel van Deventer | Journalist: Hendrik Hancke| Director: Stenette Grosskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


LINK The mighty Avodado - it’s a superfood rich in nutrients, fibre and the good fats. It is trendy and popular with the health conscious, weight-watchers, plant-based eaters… and poachers...
Howard Blight It's a huge problem. Avos make quick money, sold on the street.
V/O A founding member of SAAGA - the South African Avo Growers Association, Howard Blight, is a farmer in the Politsi Valley just outside Tzaneen in the Limpopo Province. Large-scale crop theft affects all farmers, he says.
Howard Blight It runs into hundreds of millions of rands. Stealing of avocados is not unique to South Africa. There are mafias, bosses, mafia bosses running cartels of avo theft, stealing truckloads of avocados in Mexico. They call it the Greengold.
V/O Over the past three decades consumer demand for avocados has grown internationally, with South Africans first jumping on the avo-bandwagon around 2009. According to a tree census done by SAAGA in 2020, about 15,000ha was planted with avos last year, mainly in the Limpopo Province and Mpumalanga.
Howard Blight Limpopo probably produces 65 percent of all avos in the country, mainly in the Tzaneen area and in the Levubu, Louis Trichardt area.

V/O The mild climate, rich soil and high rainfall makes this area particularly good for avos, but that does not mean that the production of world-class avocados is an easy job.
Nelius Human It's not just you plant a tree and you produce an avo. You've got a lot of things working against. You've got the weather, you've got hail, you've got wind...
V/O Second generation farmer, Nelius Human, manages about 80ha of high-production avo orchards on the outskirts of Tzaneen.
Neluis Human To produce an orchard like this, it's not cheap. Per hectare, to develop is around about R380,000 per year. Oh that that is not inclusive the tree.

Nelius Human Claire: So then tell me about the poaching problem on your farm. How long has it been happening and can you describe how bad it has affected you?

Nelius: So we've been having a massive theft problem for the last four years because the avo industry has just boomed up. Everyone wants to have it.
V/O Increased demand coupled with high prices means that brazen thieves will stop at nothing to get their hands on the crop, often damaging the fruit in the process.
Neluis - Stolen fruit demo! So they will come and they will snap it like this…

Claire: Don’t take so many! I know the farmer.

This is what happens when it’s not harvested correctly. So it will rot here in the front.
V/O Harvesting avos correctly takes patience, one needs to wait for the fruit’s moisture content to be just right, and then carefully cut it from the branch.
Nelius Stolen Fruit That stem…

Claire: Yes

That’s how I identify they stole from the orchard.

Claire: I see...
V/O The poachers don’t just make off with fruit, Human says they often lose small trees too.
Upsound Claire: What?

Yes… Yes they steal trees out of the ground while you plant them!
Neluis Human If I catch someone in the orchard stealing a checkers bag, I'm not going to be so furious about it because maybe this person doesn't have food or he doesn't have a job, but when it starts coming in 80 kg bags and bakkie loads, then it then it starts to ruin your pocket. We worked it out for the whole operation, we get up to R600,000 loss a year.
V/O On top of the losses, farmers fear that the illegal trade in damaged and unripe fruit, gives avocados a bad reputation with the consumer.
Howard Blight The thieves are picking avocados that are not mature yet. They're picking immature avocados, before we start picking. And those are going onto the street and they're going into Johannesburg. And the consumer is buying a product which doesn't give them satisfaction.
LINK Many people opt for smaller, informal markets for t heir fresh produce, but cheaper sometimes mean substandard quality and it comes at the expense of the farmer...
V/O It is in markets like these, or roadside stalls where the stolen avos reach the consumers, but understandably the traders are camera-shy.
Trader Claire: Can I ask you why you don’t want to talk?
I’m afraid. I don’t know what you want to talk about and I don’t know you….
LINK They feel very uncomfortable speaking to us. They said that they don’t know where the fruit comes from. They actually want us to speak to the owner. So I am going to try and see if I can speak to somebody else here who is selling their fruits and avocados in this market.
Upsound We’re going to the next one!
V/O This trader, who didn’t give us his name, says he’s a businessman. If someone has avos for sale, he buys it...
Trader Claire: How much is one of your bags?

It depends if it’s ripe or if it’s green, and it depends on what type of avocado are we selling...
V/O He says he only makes enough to get by, and insists that it is not his responsibility to check the origins of the fruit.
Trader I’m not guilty, I did not go to the farmer, broke the fence and steal the avocados. It’s their workers, they come through to us.
V/O He puts the blame on farm workers and even security companies...
Marius Jacobs
Canine Security I agree 100 percent of that is happening. We actually caught another security company basically stealing avos on the Agatha side when you drove to Nelius today. We found a bakkie, fully loaded with the security guard carrying a carton, a crate to the bakkie with avos on it.
V/O Marius Jacobs is the Operation Manager at Canine Security, specializing in safeguarding crops in the Tzaneen area. He says mostly they’re up against organised syndicates.
Marius Jacobs
Canine Security It's definitely a team, the team that came in here at that hole was 10 guys... and it takes them half an hour to fill up the bags.
Claire: Are these poachers dangerous? Are they armed? Do they defend themselves when they see you guys coming?
They definitely do. We had a few incidents where our guards got hurt, where the guys are armed with pangas and slashers and knives, even with firearms.
V/O A 2018 survey revealed that 83% of avo growers countrywide indicated that crop theft was a problem on their farms. An estimated 1500 tonnes of avocados - to the value of R24 million - was stolen that year, and farmers insist this number is rising.
Howard Blight Claire: And then what are farmers doing to try and mitigate the loss of all of these avos that just in terms of protecting their crops, what are farmers resorting to?
Farmers first line of defense is to put up an electric fence, our whole farm is electric fenced here...
V/O But many farmers cannot afford to install hundreds or thousands of metres of electric fence… And it’s no longer enough to keep the poachers out.
Howard Blight There are security companies now that will lease out people, trained security people, that walk the boundaries of the farm.
People in uniforms, carrying guns, walking around at night, securing the crop, 20, 20 per cent of your of your of your labor force is in security. That's high, that's high.

V/O Some even use bloodhounds to help track the poachers.
Craig Coppen We don't use the dogs for every occasion, but we have them on standby for when things get ugly.

V/O Craig Coppen manages the dog unit at Canine Security.
Craig Coppen They’re man-trailing dogs so they'll stick to human scent. So they'll usually take us to where a vehicle may be picking the thugs up. So that's the main reason is just to be able to to pursue and be able to stay on on human on human scent, in pitch darkness.
V/O But 24-hour security with highly trained dogs, state-of-the-art alarms and electric fencing come at a price...
Marius Jacobs Claire: So then when we're talking about a farm being protected from poachers and we are thinking of security at the best top tier level, how much does that cost the farmer?
You're talking about hundreds of thousands of rands. If you take I will take the example without calling a name now. But the farmer that we are protecting, maybe six farms costing R200,000 a month just on guarding.
Mandla We are small farmers, we cannot afford to have security patrolling, but that would be an ideal thing.
V/O Ten years ago Mandla Mooko traded the big-city corporate world for a peaceful life overlooking the Modjadjiskloof.
Mandla Mandla: This is the Fuerte block here.

Claire: Ah, I’m seeing Avos yes. And so when will these be fine?

Mandla: This will be fine around June, July...
V/O But even a small farm comes with big obstacles.
Mandla I believe the challenges are even more for a small farmer than for a big farmer. It’s not like you’re making a lot of money out of it. There’s a little that you get. Now if someone comes and steals that little margin has disappeared immediately.
V/O Like so many others, Mooko is doing what he can to protect his crop… but they need an urgent intervention by the authorities, says Blight.
Howard Blight The police are not showing the type of commitment that we need. They were more interested in the fruit that was being stolen because they get those avocados to eat.
V/O Ideally, Blight says, there needs to be cooperation between farmers and the police to address the situation effectively, because it ultimately affects not just the growers, but the consumers too.
Howard Blight There needs to be a process whereby the hawkers know that the growers and the authorities are making some effort to monitor the process and find out where the origins of all this fruit is coming from. At the moment, nothing's happening. So it's a free for all.

Mandla Claire: When you see these market stalls on the side of the road and people are there selling avocados… do you ever wonder, eish, those could be some of my avos?

Look it’s a bit difficult to generalise because I know along the road there are people, there are honest people also who go to the packhouse, buy their fruit to sell. So we cannot paint all of them with one brush. Yes, there are times when, especially early in the season, around January, early February, when you see a fruit, you always feel bad. I mean someone is losing money thinking they are supporting someone but that avocado could be stolen.


PROMO 1 Armed guards, alarm systems and electric fencing. Avocados have become so sought-after that syndicates are walking away with bakkie-loads at a time at expense of the farmer and the consumer...

PROMO 2 The mighty avocado has become a trendy kitchen staple and a high-value crop, attracting crime syndicates who make off with tonnes of fruit a week. What does it take to protect avos?

PROMO 3 Have you ever wondered why the avos you buy from the side of the road are often not what you expect? Hard, yet watery... or even rotting? Well, the answer lies in the picking...

So we cannot paint all of them with one brush. Yes, there are times when, especially early in the season, around January, early February, when you see a fruit, you always feel bad. I mean someone is losing money thinking they are supporting someone but that avocado could be stolen. PROMO 1 Armed guards, alarm systems and electric fencing. Avocados have become so sought-after that syndicates are walking away with bakkie-loads at a time at expense of the farmer and the consumer... PROMO 2 The mighty avocado has become a trendy kitchen staple and a high-value crop, attracting crime syndicates who make off with tonnes of fruit a week. What does it take to protect avos? PROMO 3 Have you ever wondered why the avos you buy from the side of the road are often not what you expect? Hard, yet watery... or even rotting? Well, the answer lies in the picking...

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The avocado farming industry buckles under massive pressure due to large scale avocado stealing syndicate.
metadata.Summary: The avocado farming industry are under massive pressure due to large scale theft of their produce. Since 2009, total plantings of Avocado in SA has increased due to a growing customer demand. SA produces more than 120,000 tonnes of avos annually - about 58% of our Avocados are grown in Limpopo Province To prepare land for the planting of avo’s the cost (including the planting itself and spraying of the trees) can run as much as R350 000 per hectare. Further production costs from seedling to harvest will run as much as R51 000 per hectare. A ton of stolen avo’s (depending on market prices at the time) can mean about R50 000 disappearing from a farmer’s cash flow. One ton can disappear in a single evening. But how possible is it to steal that large an amount of fruit? We will interview some farmers, as well as someone from the Avo-growers Association to discuss the modus operandi of the thieves and the implications on the industry. Introduction to viewers: * Link with Claire — making smashed avo on toast — explaining that Avocado is a superfood, popular with health conscious, weight watchers and plant-based eaters… And also… poachers…
metadata.Further information: With limited police resources,Canine Security is a wonderful outfit in the Tzaneen area. They have established a WhatsApp group for residents and respond to every call for help sent out on the group, regardless of whether the complainant is a customer of theirs or not. They have the same attitude to the farming community. We will talk to their two owners about their nightly battles against fruit thieves. A major problem in this is the fruit stalls next to our roads. A large percentage of these fruit sellers are alleged to buy from the thieves. At the moment, in that area no avo’s are ready to be picked. We will have a farmer show us how to recognize avo’s that were picked too early. - Nelius Human We will also speak to some of the informal traders, finding out where they get their avos and how much they make from the sale of their avos.
